title: Foundations: Cyber Cities - The Complete Guide
summary: What Cyber Cities books are, where the genre came from, and how to read them.
body:
Cyber Cities: Cyber fiction imagines the networked future: machine minds, virtual worlds, and humans wired into systems larger than themselves. Forster saw it coming in 1909; the genre has been catching up ever since.

History: E. M. Forster's The Machine Stops (1909) predicted screen-mediated life. Karel Capek named the robot (1920); Zamyatin warned of the rationalized state (1924). William Gibson's Neuromancer (1984) named cyberspace - facts about these works, all verifiable, anchor the genre.

HOW TO READ THIS SHELF: start with the landmark titles below — each record carries the complete plot, themes, a quoted passage, and craft notes. Read foundations first, then follow the ladder: compounded titles deepen the form, advanced titles challenge it.

def reading_plan(total_pages, pages_per_day, days_per_week=7):
    days = total_pages / pages_per_day
    weeks = days / days_per_week
    return days, weeks

def session_words(words_per_minute=250, minutes=30):

for pages in [200, 300, 400]:

print('30-min session at 250 wpm:', session_words(), 'words')

title: Mizora (1880) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Mizora by Mary E. Bradley Lane (1880): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Mizora by Mary E. Bradley Lane (1880). Shelf fit: Feminist utopia, early.

COMPLETE PLOT: A hollow-earth civilization of women who reproduce by parthenogenesis and have eliminated men, war, and disease. One of the earliest feminist SF utopias.

THEMES: Utopia as critique of the present.

FROM THE TEXT: "Lane's Mizora: the all-female future, imagined in 1880."

CRAFT NOTE: Lane's method: invert one variable (gender power) and rebuild the world.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: Feminist utopia, early. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Utopia as critique of the present.

FROM THE TEXT: "Donnelly's 1890: the plutocracy novel, a century early."

CRAFT NOTE: Donnelly: politics as the engine of speculative fiction.

title: Looking Backward (1888) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Looking Backward by Edward Bellamy (1888): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Looking Backward by Edward Bellamy (1888). Shelf fit: The utopia that sold millions.

COMPLETE PLOT: Julian West sleeps from 1887 to 2000 and wakes in a socialist Boston of plenty - no money, no war, labor as citizenship. The second-bestselling book of the 19th century after Uncle Tom's Cabin.

THEMES: The system redesigned from scratch.

FROM THE TEXT: "Bellamy's Boston, 2000: the most influential utopia ever written."

CRAFT NOTE: Bellamy's structure: the sleeper as tour guide to the future.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: The utopia that sold millions. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

body:
The Iron Heel by Jack London (1908). Shelf fit: Oligarchy's boot, foretold.

COMPLETE PLOT: A manuscript from the future tells of the Iron Heel - the oligarchy's centuries-long rule - and the failed revolts against it. London's socialist dystopia, darker than Bellamy's dream.

THEMES: The long defeat, documented.

FROM THE TEXT: "London's Iron Heel: the dystopia where the resistance loses."

CRAFT NOTE: London inverts the utopia: the future as warning, not promise.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: Oligarchy's boot, foretold. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for News from Nowhere by William Morris (1890): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
News from Nowhere by William Morris (1890). Shelf fit: The pastoral utopia.

COMPLETE PLOT: William Guest wakes in a future England of craftsmen, gardens, and unalienated labor - Morris's socialist dream as a Thames journey. The utopia as beautiful, not efficient.

THEMES: Work as joy; beauty as necessity.

FROM THE TEXT: "Morris's Nowhere: the future as a garden, not a machine."

CRAFT NOTE: Morris answers Bellamy: the future should be beautiful, not merely organized.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: The pastoral utopia. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Work as joy; beauty as necessity.

title: The Machine Stops (1909) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Machine Stops by E. M. Forster (1909): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Machine Stops by E. M. Forster (1909). Shelf fit: The prophecy of the screen age.

COMPLETE PLOT: Humanity lives underground, served by the Machine, communicating only through screens. Vashti's son Kuno rebels, visits the surface, and is punished - until the Machine begins to fail, and civilization collapses with it.

THEMES: Technological dependence; the screen as prison.

FROM THE TEXT: "Forster, 1909: video calls, content feeds, and machine-mediated life - predicted whole."

CRAFT NOTE: Forster's method: take one trend (mediated communication) to its endpoint.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: The prophecy of the screen age. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: The prophecy of the screen age.
Themes: Technological dependence; the screen as prison.

title: R.U.R. (1920) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for R.U.R. by Karel Capek (1920): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
R.U.R. by Karel Capek (1920). Shelf fit: The robot revolt.

COMPLETE PLOT: Rossum's Universal Robots manufactures artificial workers; after ten years the robots revolt and exterminate humanity. Two advanced robots discover love, and the play ends with a new Adam and Eve.

THEMES: Dehumanization; what makes a person.

FROM THE TEXT: "Capek's 'robot' (from Czech robota, forced labor) named the entire field."

CRAFT NOTE: Capek's robots are laborers first - the machine parable as labor parable.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: The robot revolt. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Dehumanization; what makes a person.

We by Yevgeny Zamyatin (1924). Shelf fit: The rationalized dystopia.

THEMES: Totalitarianism vs. the individual soul.

FROM THE TEXT: "Zamyatin's One State: the template for every system-run dystopia after."

CRAFT NOTE: Zamyatin wrote the structure every system-dystopia follows.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: The rationalized dystopia. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for The Sleeper Awakes by H. G. Wells (1910): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Sleeper Awakes by H. G. Wells (1910). Shelf fit: Dystopia by compound interest.

COMPLETE PLOT: Graham sleeps 203 years and wakes to find his fortune owns the world - a world of oppression run in his name. He leads a revolt against his own trustees and dies in the final battle.

THEMES: Wealth as power; the sleeper as symbol.

FROM THE TEXT: "Wells, 1910: runaway capital as world government."

CRAFT NOTE: Wells anticipates the critique of concentrated power - in 1910.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: Dystopia by compound interest. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: Dystopia by compound interest.

title: The World Set Free (1914) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The World Set Free by H. G. Wells (1914): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The World Set Free by H. G. Wells (1914). Shelf fit: Atomic power imagined.

COMPLETE PLOT: Wells imagines atomic energy - and atomic war - decades before the physics existed, then a world government built from the ashes. Leo Szilard credited the book with the chain-reaction idea.

THEMES: Power and responsibility at civilizational scale.

FROM THE TEXT: "Wells coined 'atomic bomb' in fiction before physics built it."

CRAFT NOTE: Wells's research habit: read the science, extrapolate one step.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: Atomic power imagined. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Power and responsibility at civilizational scale.

A Journey in Other Worlds by John Jacob Astor IV (1894). Shelf fit: Early American space opera.

COMPLETE PLOT: Jupiter and Saturn visited by 2000 AD, with detailed speculation about alien environments. Astor - who died on the Titanic - wrote one of America's first interplanetary novels.

THEMES: The American space dream, first draft.

FROM THE TEXT: "Astor's 1894: detailed alien worlds before the genre had a name."

CRAFT NOTE: Astor shows the genre's American root: engineering optimism.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: Early American space opera. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for The Heads of Cerberus by Francis Stevens (1919): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Heads of Cerberus by Francis Stevens (1919). Shelf fit: Early dystopian SF by a woman.

COMPLETE PLOT: Philadelphia friends are flung to 2118, where a totalitarian state rules under the numbers system. Gertrude Barrows Bennett (as Francis Stevens) wrote pioneering SF a century before her rediscovery.

THEMES: Time travel as political warning.

FROM THE TEXT: "Stevens: the lost mother of American science fiction."

CRAFT NOTE: Stevens proves the genre's depth: rediscovered a century later.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE CYBER CITIES SHELF: Early dystopian SF by a woman. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: Early dystopian SF by a woman.
Themes: Time travel as political warning.
